strengths: Introduces a well-designed, scaled-up behavioral benchmark (1020 trials, 255 images, eye-tracking controlled fixation) for object grouping in naturalistic scenes, going beyond prior small-scale psychophysics studies with hand-picked simple stimuli.
The two-dot paradigm with matched same/different and close/far distance conditions is methodologically careful, controlling for confounds like distance alone driving judgments.

Proposes a simple and interpretable object-centricity metric (ROC/AUC over patch affinity maps against ground-truth object boundaries) that does not require additional supervision and is applied consistently across models and layers/heads.

Evaluates a reasonably diverse set of models (DINO family, MAE, supervised ViT, ConvNext, distilled ConvNext) revealing a clear and consistent trend that self-supervised DINO-style objectives yield stronger object-centric structure and behavioral alignment than supervised training, with reasonable control for architecture confound.

The Gram-matrix distillation experiment is a nice causal/interventional test (rather than purely correlational) showing that explicitly aligning Gram structure improves both object-centricity and behavioral alignment, strengthening the causal claim beyond correlation in Fig. 6B.
Results are convergent with independent literature on DINOv3's Gram anchoring mechanism, lending external validity to the interpretation.
Human behavioral results replicate known effects (same-object advantage, distance effects) validating the dataset and task design.
weaknesses: The behavioral sample is homogeneous (72 undergraduates from one institution) and the stimulus set, while larger than prior work, is still limited to a filtered subset of COCO images with clear central-object boundaries, which may limit generalizability of findings to more cluttered/ambiguous real-world scenes.

Only ViT-Base scale models are compared for most architectures (with some ConvNext-Base); the paper does not systematically vary model size to disentangle scale effects from training objective effects, despite claiming objective is more important than architecture — a single size point weakens this claim.

The MLP readout approach for predicting same/different judgments and RTs is somewhat ad hoc; the relationship between classifier probability/logit and RT is not explicitly justified (how is accuracy translated to RT predictions?), and details of the RT-prediction MLP (loss function, exact input features) are sparse.

The Gram-alignment fine-tuning experiment lacks methodological detail (loss weighting, training duration, which layers are distilled, how much ImageNet performance is retained) needed for reproducibility, and only tests 4 models without ablating the distillation coefficient or alternative distillation targets (e.g., non-Gram feature distillation baseline) to isolate the specific contribution of Gram-matrix matching versus generic feature distillation from DINOv3.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, bootstrap tests) is reported for the correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment (Fig 6B) or between conditions in Fig 2D/4A, making it hard to assess robustness of some claims, especially given the modest number of models (9) used for the AUC vs. alignment correlation.

The paper claims 'human-like' object grouping and draws strong conclusions about biological plausibility, but does not compare against any explicit low-level Gestalt/heuristic baselines (e.g., simple color/texture similarity, superpixel segmentation, or classical grouping cues) to contextualize how much of the alignment is trivially explained by non-semantic low-level similarity versus genuinely object-centric/semantic structure.
The discussion of why Transformer architectures benefit more from Gram alignment than ConvNext is speculative and not directly tested with additional analysis (e.g., ablating attention mechanism).

strengths: Introduces a substantial, well-controlled behavioral dataset (72 subjects, 1020 trials, eye-tracking enforced fixation) that meaningfully scales up a classical two-dot psychophysics paradigm to naturalistic COCO images, providing a valuable resource for the community.

Careful experimental design, including matched same/different distances to rule out simple distance confounds, manual verification of object boundaries, and eye-tracking-based fixation control, lends strong credibility to the behavioral data.

The proposed ROC-based object-centricity metric is simple, interpretable, and requires no additional supervision, making it broadly applicable for probing patch-level representations in any vision model.

The comparison across a well-chosen diverse set of models (DINO family, MAE, supervised ViT/ConvNeXt, distilled ConvNeXt) isolates the effect of training objective versus architecture in a clean, controlled manner, yielding a clear and consistent finding (objective > architecture).

The Gram-alignment distillation experiment is a nice causal/interventional complement to the correlational analyses, and its convergence with DINOv3's own reported motivation for Gram anchoring strengthens the paper's mechanistic claims.
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the figures (affinity maps, ROC curves, behavioral condition breakdowns) effectively support the narrative.
weaknesses: Only ViT-Base and ConvNeXt-Base are tested; there is no exploration of model scale (e.g., ViT-L/g or larger DINOv3 variants) which could confound 'objective' effects with capacity, and would strengthen claims about generality.

The readout used to predict same/different judgments and RTs is a simple 2-layer MLP trained on ~30k COCO-derived synthetic trials; details of this readout (architecture, training details, hyperparameter selection, sensitivity to design choices) are sparse, limiting reproducibility and interpretability of the reported grouping accuracies and correlations.

The Gram-alignment distillation procedure (loss formulation, training schedule, hyperparameters, and whether ImageNet classification accuracy is preserved) is not described in sufficient detail in the main text, making the central mechanistic claim harder to fully verify or reproduce.

Statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals or significance tests comparing models' normalized Spearman correlations, or the object-centricity vs. behavioral-alignment correlation in Fig. 6B) is not reported, so the strength of some comparisons (e.g., DINOv3 vs DINOv2 ViT-B) is unclear.

The behavioral paradigm, while scaled up relative to prior work, still only samples two dot locations per image (center + one peripheral point) and does not capture the full richness of object segmentation (e.g., full-scene segmentation, multi-part object structure), which somewhat limits how strongly the object-centricity metric's real segmentation validity can be assessed against exhaustive human judgments.

The paper would benefit from more direct comparison to other alignment approaches or brain-based benchmarks (e.g., referenced fMRI encoding results) to contextualize how large the reported behavioral alignment gap to the noise ceiling actually is in absolute terms.

strengths: Introduces a well-designed, large-scale behavioral benchmark using a classical two-dot object-grouping paradigm scaled to >1000 trials across 255 naturalistic COCO images, with careful controls (eye-tracking with fixation enforcement, counterbalanced same/different and close/far conditions, matched distances to rule out simple distance confounds).

Proposes a novel, label-free object-centricity metric based on ROC analysis of patch affinity maps that is interpretable and directly tied to ground-truth object boundaries, and shows it correlates strongly (Spearman r=0.95) with behavioral alignment across a diverse set of 9 models.

The Gram-matrix distillation experiment is a genuine causal manipulation (rather than purely correlational), demonstrating that explicitly aligning pairwise patch similarity structure of supervised models with a self-supervised teacher improves both object-centricity and behavioral alignment, while a CLS-token distillation control convincingly isolates Gram structure as the relevant mechanism.

Strong methodological rigor in the modeling pipeline: nested cross-validation, noise-ceiling normalization of behavioral correlations, a linear-readout robustness check, and condition-wise correlation breakdowns that support that alignment findings are not artifacts of readout capacity or a single condition.

Convincingly reproduces qualitative human behavioral signatures (same-object advantage, distance effect specific to same-object trials) in model predictions, strengthening the claim of human-like grouping.

Clear connection to relevant literature in both computer vision (DINO family, MAE, LOST/TokenCut) and visual neuroscience/psychophysics (association fields, Gestalt grouping, same-object advantage), situating the contribution well.
weaknesses: The model sample is small (9 models, mostly ViT-B/ConvNext-B variants), and the striking r=0.95 correlation between object-centricity and behavioral alignment should be interpreted cautiously given so few data points and no held-out model families (e.g., no CLIP, no larger/smaller scale variants) to test generalization of the relationship.

Training objective and architecture/data-scale are not fully decoupled (as the paper itself acknowledges); with only one model per cell of the design, it is hard to cleanly attribute effects to objective versus scale versus architecture.

The behavioral measure is restricted to RT in a single two-dot same/different judgment; while well validated, this is still a narrow operationalization of "human-like object grouping," and it remains unclear how well findings would generalize to other measures of segmentation behavior (e.g., explicit boundary tracing, multi-object scenes).

The MLP readout for grouping/RT prediction is trained on ~30,000 synthetic trials derived from the same dot-placement algorithm and COCO annotations used to build the behavioral stimuli, raising some concern about whether learned readouts pick up on dataset-specific regularities in COCO annotations rather than purely general object-centric structure.

Gram alignment fine-tunes only the last transformer/conv block with a single teacher (DINOv3 ViT-B) and a single loss weighting; no ablation of layer depth, distillation strength, or alternative teachers is provided, limiting insight into the generality/robustness of the mechanism.

Some interpretive claims in the conclusion (e.g., that the path to perceptually aligned models lies in "explicitly shaping similarity structure" rather than "scaling classification objectives") are somewhat strong given the limited set of models and single dataset/benchmark used to support them.

No explicit statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported for the key AUC-behavioral alignment correlation (r=0.95, p=0.0001) beyond the p-value itself, e.g., bootstrap CIs over model subsets, which would help contextualize robustness given n=9.

strengths: Large-scale, well-controlled behavioral benchmark: scales a classical same/different two-dot psychophysics paradigm from ~24 hand-picked images to 255 naturalistic COCO images and 1020 trials, with eye-tracking to enforce fixation and careful counterbalancing across conditions (same/different x close/far).

Diverse and appropriate model comparison spanning architecture (ViT vs ConvNext) and training objective (DINO family, MAE, supervised IN1K/IN21K, and a distilled ConvNext), which helps disentangle contributions of architecture vs. objective.

The proposed object-centricity metric (ROC/AUC over patch affinity maps relative to ground-truth object boundaries) is simple, label-free at inference time, and shows a strong correlation (Spearman r=0.95) with behavioral alignment across the 9 models tested.

The Gram-matrix alignment experiment provides a causal manipulation rather than purely correlational evidence: fine-tuning supervised backbones to match DINOv3's Gram structure improves grouping accuracy, object-centricity, and behavioral alignment simultaneously, while classification accuracy is unaffected.

Good use of controls to rule out confounds: a CLS-token-only distillation baseline that isolates Gram structure as the operative signal, a linear-readout baseline to show results aren't an artifact of MLP capacity, and a subject-split noise ceiling for normalizing behavioral alignment scores.
Detailed supplementary behavioral analyses (accuracy, d-prime, criterion, condition-specific correlations) support that the RT signal used for model comparison is reliable and not artifactual.
weaknesses: The correlation between object-centric AUC and behavioral alignment, while strong, is computed over only 9 models; with such a small sample the r=0.95 finding is suggestive but not highly robust to outliers or unmeasured confounds (e.g., dataset scale and architecture are entangled with training objective across this model set, as the authors themselves note).

There is a risk of circularity between the object-centricity AUC metric and the Gram-alignment manipulation: both are fundamentally measuring/optimizing patch-wise feature similarity structure, so improvements in AUC following Gram distillation may be partly definitional rather than an independent validation of behavioral relevance.

Only ViT-Base/ConvNext-Base sized models are tested; no analysis of how findings scale with model size, which limits the generality of claims about 'model generations' and architecture-objective interactions.

Model predictions of human RTs remain well below the noise ceiling for most models (normalized Spearman correlations range ~0.47–0.83), and single-trial/held-out variance explained is modest; this gap is acknowledged but not deeply analyzed (e.g., what residual behavioral variance is left unexplained by object-centric structure).

The Gram-alignment loss weighting (classification:Gram = 1:10) is chosen heuristically ('to make the two loss values comparable in scale') without an ablation showing sensitivity of the reported gains to this hyperparameter.

The behavioral benchmark is restricted to a single population (72 undergraduate students) and a specific stimulus construction (COCO images with one object overlapping the center, dot placement constrained to four conditions), which may limit generalizability to broader object-grouping phenomena or other naturalistic settings.

The MLP readout for grouping accuracy is trained on ~30,000 synthetically generated trials from the same dot-placement algorithm as the test set, which, while using held-out images, still shares generation procedure and could inflate apparent grouping accuracy relative to more naturalistic testing conditions.

Some interpretive claims (e.g., 'self-attention mechanism provides a particularly natural substrate for encoding pairwise patch relationships') are speculative and not directly tested mechanistically.
